summary: Defines a method to encrypt file transfers using the FTP specification with the KEA key exchange and SKIPJACK cipher. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a way to put a lock on file transfers using a particular government-designed lock and key kit.

questions: what is kea and skipjack ftp encryption
how to encrypt ftp commands and data
subtitle: How to secure FTP file transfers using KEA authentication and SKIPJACK encryption.

tldr.problem: FTP sends passwords in the clear and provides no protection for file transfers after initial authentication, making file transfers vulnerable to eavesdropping and tampering.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC profiles the use of KEA (Key Exchange Algorithm) for mutual authentication and SKIPJACK symmetric encryption for protecting both FTP commands and file data, working within the FTP Security Extensions framework defined in RFC 2228.
tldr.outcome: The specification remained experimental and saw limited adoption. Modern file transfer has largely moved to SFTP (over SSH) and HTTPS, which became more widely used standards for secure transfers.

today: RFC 2773 remained experimental and saw limited deployment. The use of SKIPJACK (a government-designed cipher) and KEA faced skepticism in the cryptographic community. Modern secure file transfer has converged on SFTP (over SSH) and HTTPS, which have become more widely supported standards. FTP itself is rarely used on public networks today.

sections.title: FTP and Its Security Gaps
sections.content:
The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) is one of the oldest Internet protocols, but it has a critical weakness: it offers almost no security. User passwords are sent in the clear (unencrypted), and there is no protection for the actual file data during transfer. An attacker on the network can read everything: passwords, file contents, and commands.

RFC 2228 (FTP Security Extensions) solved this by providing a framework that lets FTP implementations use different security mechanisms. RFC 2773 defines one such mechanism: a profile using the KEA key exchange algorithm for authentication and the SKIPJACK cipher for encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Old FTP is like sending postcards—anyone can read them. This RFC adds locked envelopes using two cryptography tools: KEA to prove who you are, and SKIPJACK to scramble what you send.

sections.title: Key Exchange and Mutual Authentication
sections.content:
The KEA (Key Exchange Algorithm) serves two purposes in this profile: it allows the FTP client and server to authenticate each other, and it allows them to establish shared encryption keys.

The process begins when the client sends AUTH KEA-SKIPJACK. The server responds with its certificate (containing its KEA public key) and a random number. The client, using its own certificate and private key, computes a shared secret with the server using KEA. The client also generates two additional keys: the MEK (Message Encryption Key) for protecting commands and the TEK (Token Encryption Key) for wrapping other keys. These keys are sent to the server wrapped in the TEK for confidentiality. The client also sends an optional list of security labels. At the end, both parties have verified each other's identity and share the symmetric keys needed for encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server shake hands using secret keys only they know. They prove who they are by showing signed certificates, then they agree on a secret encryption key to use from now on.

sections.title: Command and File Encryption
sections.content:
Once authenticated and keys are established, all FTP commands are encrypted using SKIPJACK in CBC mode. Each command is protected with a sequence number and an ICV (Integrity Check Value) to detect tampering. The sequence number is incremented for each command, and the server echoes it back to ensure command ordering.

File data is transferred in buffers. Each transfer is preceded by a token containing the FEK (File Encryption Key), a hash of the complete file for integrity checking, an initialization vector (IV), and the security label. The FEK can be different for each file, or the same FEK can be reused for pre-encrypted files. All padding follows the standard rule: append n octets of value n to make the plaintext a multiple of 8 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every command gets a sequence number so the server knows if any got lost or reordered. Every file gets its own key and a checksum to make sure it did not get changed.

sections.title: Protocol Message Flows
sections.content: The RFC documents the complete protocol flow with example message sequences. After authentication and key agreement, the client issues protected commands using the ENC prefix followed by Base64-encoded encrypted data. The first exchange typically negotiates the buffer size using PBSZ (Protection Buffer Size), followed by user authentication with USER and PASS commands, all encrypted under the MEK. The PROT command specifies that data transfers should be protected. When the client retrieves a file with RETR, the server sends the encryption token first, followed by encrypted file data. The token is sent on the data channel to avoid ordering dependencies with the command channel.
sections.plainLanguage: The conversation happens in a fixed order: first agree on buffer sizes, then log in with encrypted passwords, then request files which arrive with their own encryption key attached.

sections.title: Security and Key Protection
sections.content:
The security of this system depends entirely on keeping private keys secret and shared symmetric keys protected from disclosure. The implementation must ensure that the KEA private key (used to derive the session key) never leaves the system and that the SKIPJACK keys (MEK, TEK, and FEK) are kept in memory securely. Loss or compromise of a private key allows an attacker to decrypt all session traffic.

For pre-encrypted files, the RFC suggests that file encryption keys be wrapped in a local storage key when at rest in the file system. Only when a file needs to be transferred is the FEK unwrapped and rewrapped in the current session TEK.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone steals the secret keys, they can read everything. Implementations must protect keys as carefully as they would protect a password or credit card number.
